claim: Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) has quickly gained popularity as a powerful tool for eliciting genetically targeted neuronal activation.
source: Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) has quickly gained popularity as a powerful tool for eliciting genetically targeted neuronal activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the adoption and utility of ChR2 in neuroscience research, supported by established scientific knowledge and the context of the manuscript.

claim: Little has been reported on the response kinetics of optogenetic stimulation across different neuronal subtypes.
source: However, little has been reported on the response kinetics of optogenetic stimulation across different neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the literature, which is an inference based on the authors' review of existing research.

claim: With excess stimulation, neurons can be driven into depolarization block, a state where they cease to fire action potentials.
source: With excess stimulation, neurons can be driven into depolarization block, a state where they cease to fire action potentials.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neurophysiological knowledge about depolarization block.

claim: Light-induced depolarization block in neurons expressing ChR2 poses experimental challenges for stable activation of specific cell types.
source: Herein, we demonstrate that light-induced depolarization block in neurons expressing ChR2 poses experimental challenges for stable activation of specific cell types and may confound interpretation of experiments when 'activated' neurons are in fact being functionally silenced.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing depolarization block in various neuronal subtypes.

claim: Certain neuronal subtypes targeted for ChR2 expression become increasingly susceptible to depolarization block as the duration of light pulses are increased.
source: We show both ex vivo and in vivo that certain neuronal subtypes targeted for ChR2 expression become increasingly susceptible to depolarization block as the duration of light pulses are increased.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from both ex vivo and in vivo recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Interneuron populations have a greater susceptibility to depolarization block than principal excitatory neurons.
source: We find that interneuron populations have a greater susceptibility to this effect than principal excitatory neurons, which are more resistant to light-induced depolarization block.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data from recordings of different neuronal cell types presented in the manuscript.

claim: ChR2 is a seven-transmembrane-domain, nonselective cation channel that is directly activated by blue light when bound with the chromophore all-trans-retinal.
source: Isolated from the green algae, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, ChR2 is a seven-transmembrane-domain, nonselective cation channel that is directly activated by blue light when bound with the chromophore all-trans-retinal (Hegemann et al., 1991; Lawson et al., 1991; Takahashi et al., 1991; Nagel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research characterizing ChR2's molecular structure and function.

claim: ChR2 was isolated from the green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: Isolated from the green algae, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, ChR2 is a seven-transmembrane-domain, nonselective cation channel that is directly activated by blue light when bound with the chromophore all-trans-retinal (Hegemann et al., 1991; Lawson et al., 1991; Takahashi et al., 1991; Nagel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on the origin of ChR2.

claim: Absorption of photons by the chromophore induces conformational changes in the channel that allow for the passage of cations across the cell membrane.
source: Absorption of photons by the chromophore induces conformational changes in the channel that allow for the passage of cations across the cell membrane in which it is expressed (Boyden et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research describing the mechanism of ChR2 activation.

claim: Many studies using ChR2 for in vivo manipulation have largely focused on the activation of principal excitatory neurons, particularly in the cortex.
source: Many studies to date that utilized ChR2 for in vivo manipulation of behavior and/or circuit function have largely focused on the activation of principal excitatory neurons, particularly in the cortex (Petreanu et al., 2007; Huber et al., 2008; Ayling et al., 2009; Boyd et al., 2012; Britt et al., 2012; Beltramo et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous optogenetic studies.

claim: ChR2 expression, trafficking, and activation has been achieved in most types of nervous tissue.
source: Although ChR2 expression, trafficking, and activation has been achieved in most types of nervous tissue (Li et al., 2005; Nagel et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2006; Schroll et al., 2006; Adamantidis et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2007; Douglass et al., 2008; Mahoney et al., 2008; Baier and Scott, 2009; Guo et al., 2009; Han et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2009; Gourine et al., 2010; Hagglund et al., 2010; Diester and et al, 2011; Figueiredo et al., 2011; Sasaki et al., 2012; Ljaschenko et al., 2013), little consideration has been given to the kinetics that constrain light-induced firing properties in different neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous research demonstrating ChR2 expression across various nervous tissues.

claim: Little consideration has been given to the kinetics that constrain light-induced firing properties in different neuronal subtypes.
source: Although ChR2 expression, trafficking, and activation has been achieved in most types of nervous tissue (Li et al., 2005; Nagel et al., 2005; Bi et al., 2006; Schroll et al., 2006; Adamantidis et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2007; Douglass et al., 2008; Mahoney et al., 2008; Baier and Scott, 2009; Guo et al., 2009; Han et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2009; Gourine et al., 2010; Hagglund et al., 2010; Diester and et al, 2011; Figueiredo et al., 2011; Sasaki et al., 2012; Ljaschenko et al., 2013), little consideration has been given to the kinetics that constrain light-induced firing properties in different neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' review of the literature, identifying a gap in knowledge.

claim: Factors that affect the degree of neuronal photostimulation, including intrinsic differences in firing dynamics, membrane properties, and channel composition differ among neuronal cell types.
source: Factors that affect the degree of neuronal photostimulation, including intrinsic differences in firing dynamics, membrane properties, and channel composition differ among neuronal cell types.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of neuronal biophysics and cellular diversity.

claim: These properties render certain neuronal populations more susceptible to depolarization block.
source: These properties render certain neuronal populations more susceptible to depolarization block, which is generally induced by excessive cation influx, prolonged membrane depolarization, and/or the inability to repolarize, resulting in the failure to support continuous firing of action potentials.
evidence: This is an inference based on known neurophysiological principles and the experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Depolarization block is generally induced by excessive cation influx, prolonged membrane depolarization, and/or the inability to repolarize, resulting in the failure to support continuous firing of action potentials.
source: These properties render certain neuronal populations more susceptible to depolarization block, which is generally induced by excessive cation influx, prolonged membrane depolarization, and/or the inability to repolarize, resulting in the failure to support continuous firing of action potentials.
evidence: This claim is based on established neurophysiological knowledge about the mechanisms of depolarization block.

claim: In vitro electrophysiological recordings have shown the ability of ultrafast microbial opsins to inactivate neurons via excessive photo-induced currents.
source: In vitro electrophysiological recordings have shown the ability of ultrafast microbial opsins to inactivate neurons via excessive photo-induced currents, where regular-spiking excitatory neurons showed a greater tendency to enter depolarization block than fast-spiking interneurons (Mattis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Regular-spiking excitatory neurons showed a greater tendency to enter depolarization block than fast-spiking interneurons in response to ultrafast microbial opsins.
source: In vitro electrophysiological recordings have shown the ability of ultrafast microbial opsins to inactivate neurons via excessive photo-induced currents, where regular-spiking excitatory neurons showed a greater tendency to enter depolarization block than fast-spiking interneurons (Mattis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research by Mattis et al., 2012.

claim: Recent studies in primary hippocampal cultures have explored the effect of different ChR2 variants on neuronal firing properties in response to differing light intensity and pulse duration.
source: Similarly, recent studies in primary hippocampal cultures have explored the effect of different ChR2 variants on neuronal firing properties in response to differing light intensity and pulse duration (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research by Lin et al., 2013.

claim: Multiple ChR2 mouse lines expressed the common ChR2 variant (H134R).
source: Using multiple ChR2 mouse lines that expressed the common ChR2 variant (H134R), we show both ex vivo and in vivo that light-induced neuronal firing can be accompanied and/or followed with periods of latency in various neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental model used in the study.

claim: Light-induced neuronal firing can be accompanied and/or followed with periods of latency in various neuronal subtypes.
source: Using multiple ChR2 mouse lines that expressed the common ChR2 variant (H134R), we show both ex vivo and in vivo that light-induced neuronal firing can be accompanied and/or followed with periods of latency in various neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both ex vivo and in vivo recordings.

claim: Interneurons are particularly vulnerable to light-induced depolarization block.
source: Further, we show that interneurons are particularly vulnerable to this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different neuronal cell types.

claim: At a fixed moderate frequency of light stimulation, increasing pulse width resulted in transient activation and protracted silencing of regular-spiking interneurons.
source: In particular, at a fixed moderate frequency of light stimulation, increasing pulse width resulted in transient activation and protracted silencing of regular-spiking interneurons, but excitatory principal/pyramidal cells or subsets of fast-spiking neuronal populations were more resistant to depolarization block.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of regular-spiking interneurons.

claim: Excitatory principal/pyramidal cells or subsets of fast-spiking neuronal populations were more resistant to depolarization block than regular-spiking interneurons.
source: In particular, at a fixed moderate frequency of light stimulation, increasing pulse width resulted in transient activation and protracted silencing of regular-spiking interneurons, but excitatory principal/pyramidal cells or subsets of fast-spiking neuronal populations were more resistant to depolarization block.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data from different neuronal cell types.

claim: The duration of a light pulse beyond a certain point, independent of frequency, fails to result in higher spike rates in neurons expressing ChR2, but rather silences them.
source: Additionally, we found that the duration of a light pulse beyond a certain point, independent of frequency, fails to result in higher spike rates in neurons expressing ChR2, but rather silences them.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between pulse duration and neuronal firing.

claim: Short-width light pulses are recommended when using ChR2 for the activation of interneuron cell types.
source: Together, our data recommend the use of short-width light pulses when using ChR2 for the activation of interneuron cell types, while slightly longer pulse widths may be desirable for consistent spiking of larger excitatory cell types.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slightly longer pulse widths may be desirable for consistent spiking of larger excitatory cell types.
source: Together, our data recommend the use of short-width light pulses when using ChR2 for the activation of interneuron cell types, while slightly longer pulse widths may be desirable for consistent spiking of larger excitatory cell types.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Crh-Cre+/−; ROSA26LSL-ChR2-EYFP animals expressed the ChR2-EYFP fusion protein selectively in CRH-positive interneurons of the external plexiform layer (EPL).
source: Within the main olfactory bulb, Crh-Cre+/−; ROSA26LSL-ChR2-EYFP animals expressed the ChR2-EYFP fusion protein selectively in CRH-positive interneurons of the external plexiform layer (EPL) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and microscopy images showing ChR2-EYFP expression.

claim: For olfactory bulb CRH interneurons, short duration (5–25 ms) light pulses were optimal for sustaining consistent neuronal firing.
source: For olfactory bulb CRH interneurons, we observed that short duration (5–25 ms) light pulses ('time on') were optimal for sustaining consistent neuronal firing, with a highest average firing rate elicited at 10 ms pulse widths (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The highest average firing rate in CRH interneurons was elicited at 10 ms pulse widths.
source: For olfactory bulb CRH interneurons, we observed that short duration (5–25 ms) light pulses ('time on') were optimal for sustaining consistent neuronal firing, with a highest average firing rate elicited at 10 ms pulse widths (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Increasing the duration of a light pulse to more than 25 ms reliably decreased firing rates in CRH interneurons.
source: In contrast, increasing the duration of a light pulse to more than 25 ms, such that 'time on' pulse duration outlasted the interval between pulses ('time off'), reliably decreased firing rates, and completely silenced neurons at pulse durations of ≥49 ms 'time on' (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings and is illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: CRH interneurons were completely silenced at pulse durations of ≥49 ms.
source: In contrast, increasing the duration of a light pulse to more than 25 ms, such that 'time on' pulse duration outlasted the interval between pulses ('time off'), reliably decreased firing rates, and completely silenced neurons at pulse durations of ≥49 ms 'time on' (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings and is illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The silencing phenomenon in CRH interneurons is not likely due to desensitization of the ChR2 itself.
source: This phenomenon is not likely due to desensitization of the ChR2 itself, as stepwise current injections independent of ChR2-mediated light activation mirror silencing observed in neurons from increased light pulse duration (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current injection experiments that recapitulate the silencing effect without light activation.

claim: CRH-expressing EPL interneurons exhibit high probability (>80%) co-expression with the fast-spiking interneuron marker, parvalbumin (PV).
source: Interestingly, CRH-expressing EPL interneurons exhibit high probability (>80%) co-expression with the fast-spiking interneuron marker, parvalbumin (PV), and are capable of achieving high firing rates when stimulated by light (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research by Huang et al., 2013.

claim: CRH-expressing EPL interneurons are capable of achieving high firing rates when stimulated by light.
source: Interestingly, CRH-expressing EPL interneurons exhibit high probability (>80%) co-expression with the fast-spiking interneuron marker, parvalbumin (PV), and are capable of achieving high firing rates when stimulated by light (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research by Huang et al., 2013.

claim: CRH-expressing EPL interneurons exhibit a functional heterogeneity in their electrical responses.
source: Our present results suggest that CRH-expressing EPL interneurons exhibit a functional heterogeneity in their electrical responses, at least in a subset of neurons, highlighting the limitation of using broad neuronal markers (e.g., parvalbumin) as being indicative of a general firing response pattern (i.e., fast-spiking) that may not be generalizable from one brain region (e.g., cortex) to another (e.g., olfactory bulb).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing variable responses in CRH interneurons despite parvalbumin co-expression.

claim: Chat-ChR2 transgenic mice show expression of ChR2-EYFP in cholinergic neurons of the brain, with dense expression in the medial habenula (MHB) and throughout the striatum.
source: Chat-ChR2 transgenic mice show expression of ChR2-EYFP in cholinergic neurons of the brain, with dense expression in the medial habenula (MHB) (Figure 2A) and throughout the striatum (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and microscopy images showing ChR2-EYFP expression patterns.

claim: ChAT-positive MHB interneurons exhibited robust and consistent firing with short duration (≤25 ms) light pulses.
source: Like CRH-expressing interneurons of the olfactory bulb, ChAT-positive MHB interneurons (Figure 2C, N = 9) and striatal interneurons (Figure 2D, N = 15) exhibited robust and consistent firing with short duration (≤25 ms) light pulses, and dramatic decreases in firing rates with pulse width durations greater than 40 ms (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings of ChAT interneurons.

claim: ChAT-positive striatal interneurons exhibited robust and consistent firing with short duration (≤25 ms) light pulses.
source: Like CRH-expressing interneurons of the olfactory bulb, ChAT-positive MHB interneurons (Figure 2C, N = 9) and striatal interneurons (Figure 2D, N = 15) exhibited robust and consistent firing with short duration (≤25 ms) light pulses, and dramatic decreases in firing rates with pulse width durations greater than 40 ms (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings of ChAT interneurons.

claim: ChAT-positive MHB and striatal interneurons showed dramatic decreases in firing rates with pulse width durations greater than 40 ms.
source: Like CRH-expressing interneurons of the olfactory bulb, ChAT-positive MHB interneurons (Figure 2C, N = 9) and striatal interneurons (Figure 2D, N = 15) exhibited robust and consistent firing with short duration (≤25 ms) light pulses, and dramatic decreases in firing rates with pulse width durations greater than 40 ms (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings of ChAT interneurons.

claim: SST-expressing interneurons have been characterized as a heterogeneous population, both morphologically and electrophysiologically.
source: SST-expressing interneurons have been characterized as a heterogeneous population, both morphologically and electrophysiologically (Markram et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research characterizing SST interneurons.

claim: SST interneurons exhibit electrophysiological heterogeneity, with one subset exhibiting regular-spiking neuronal activity and another exhibiting faster-spiking dynamics.
source: Our recordings validate previous reports (Wang et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2006) of electrophysiological heterogeneity between SST cortical interneurons, with one subset of SST interneurons exhibiting regular-spiking neuronal activity and another exhibiting faster-spiking dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of SST interneurons and citations to previous research.

claim: Regular-spiking SST interneurons showed photostimulation responses consistent with those seen in CRH and ChAT interneurons.
source: The former subset showed photostimulation responses consistent with those seen in CRH and ChAT interneurons (Figure 3G–J, N = 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of regular-spiking SST interneurons.

claim: Faster-spiking SST interneurons increased their firing rates with longer light pulse duration.
source: Interestingly, faster-spiking SST interneurons (N = 9) increased their firing rates with longer light pulse duration (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of fast-spiking SST interneurons.

claim: Overall average firing rates scaled with increasing light intensities across all interneuron cell types tested.
source: Though overall average firing rates scaled with increasing light intensities across all interneuron cell types tested, increased pulse duration was sufficient to drive neurons into depolarization block regardless of light intensity (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between light intensity and firing rates.

claim: Increased pulse duration was sufficient to drive neurons into depolarization block regardless of light intensity.
source: Though overall average firing rates scaled with increasing light intensities across all interneuron cell types tested, increased pulse duration was sufficient to drive neurons into depolarization block regardless of light intensity (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings at different light intensities.

claim: Fast-spiking SST interneurons exhibited increased and sustained firing with increasing pulse duration at all four light intensities.
source: Fast-spiking SST interneurons, however, exhibited increased and sustained firing with increasing pulse duration at all four light intensities (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of fast-spiking SST interneurons at different light intensities.

claim: Regular-spiking interneurons showed decreased averaged spike amplitudes over the duration of the stimulus train in response to increased pulse widths.
source: These data are consistent with decreased averaged spike amplitudes over the duration of the stimulus train in response to increased pulse widths (Figure 4F–I), with the exception of fast-spiking SST interneurons, which showed only modest reductions in spike amplitudes over time (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike amplitudes over time.

claim: Fast-spiking SST interneurons showed only modest reductions in spike amplitudes over time.
source: These data are consistent with decreased averaged spike amplitudes over the duration of the stimulus train in response to increased pulse widths (Figure 4F–I), with the exception of fast-spiking SST interneurons, which showed only modest reductions in spike amplitudes over time (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike amplitudes in fast-spiking SST interneurons.

claim: Interneurons generally exhibited high spike probabilities with short light pulses (≤25 ms).
source: While interneurons generally exhibited high spike probabilities with short light pulses (≤25 ms), prolonged light pulses dramatically increased spike failure (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike probabilities across different pulse durations.

claim: Prolonged light pulses dramatically increased spike failure in interneurons.
source: While interneurons generally exhibited high spike probabilities with short light pulses (≤25 ms), prolonged light pulses dramatically increased spike failure (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike probabilities across different pulse durations.

claim: With long pulses, regular-spiking interneurons characteristically fired an initial action potential or a short burst of action potentials, followed by prolonged depolarization block.
source: With long pulses, regular-spiking interneurons characteristically fired an initial action potential or a short burst of action potentials, followed by prolonged depolarization block.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of firing patterns in regular-spiking interneurons.

claim: Fast-spiking SST interneurons exhibited higher spike fidelity than other interneurons tested, even with long pulses.
source: Fast-spiking SST interneurons exhibited higher spike fidelity than other interneurons tested, even with long pulses (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing spike fidelity across different interneuron types.

claim: Due to size, typical excitatory neurons have low membrane resistance.
source: Due to size, typical excitatory neurons have low membrane resistance.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of neuronal biophysics.

claim: Low membrane resistance makes excitatory neurons more resistant to depolarization block.
source: This property makes excitatory neurons more resistant to depolarization block, as changes in voltage across the membrane require higher levels of current input.
evidence: This is an inference based on established neurophysiological principles.

claim: Previous work has shown that increasing the frequency of light stimulation by various activating opsins results in decreased spike probability.
source: Previous work has shown that increasing the frequency of light stimulation by various activating opsins results in decreased spike probability (Mattis et al., 2012), consistent with known firing properties of pyramidal neurons and fast-spiking PV interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research by Mattis et al., 2012.

claim: Thy1-ChR2 mice selectively express ChR2-EYFP in mitral/tufted cells of the main olfactory bulb.
source: To test the response kinetics of light-induced firing in excitatory cell types, we next performed whole-cell recordings in brain slices from Thy1-ChR2 mice that selectively express ChR2-EYFP in mitral/tufted cells of the main olfactory bulb (Arenkiel et al., 2007) (Figure 5A), as well as in layer V cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous research describing the Thy1-ChR2 mouse line.

claim: Thy1-ChR2 mice express ChR2-EYFP in layer V cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: To test the response kinetics of light-induced firing in excitatory cell types, we next performed whole-cell recordings in brain slices from Thy1-ChR2 mice that selectively express ChR2-EYFP in mitral/tufted cells of the main olfactory bulb (Arenkiel et al., 2007) (Figure 5A), as well as in layer V cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and microscopy images.

claim: Populations of excitatory cells (mitral cells and pyramidal neurons) were more resistant to prolonged light pulse-induced depolarization block than regular-spiking interneurons.
source: In contrast to the observed inhibition reported in regular-spiking interneurons, these populations of excitatory cells were more resistant to prolonged light pulse-induced depolarization block.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data from recordings of excitatory cells and interneurons.

claim: Increased light pulse duration elicited rapid, sustained neuronal firing in mitral cells.
source: Increased light pulse duration elicited rapid, sustained neuronal firing in mitral cells (N = 14) (Figure 5C,D), whereas short pulse widths (<25 ms) appeared less effective than slightly longer pulse durations (25–49 ms) at eliciting robust spiking, likely due to low membrane resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of mitral cells.

claim: Short pulse widths (<25 ms) appeared less effective than slightly longer pulse durations (25–49 ms) at eliciting robust spiking in mitral cells, likely due to low membrane resistance.
source: Increased light pulse duration elicited rapid, sustained neuronal firing in mitral cells (N = 14) (Figure 5C,D), whereas short pulse widths (<25 ms) appeared less effective than slightly longer pulse durations (25–49 ms) at eliciting robust spiking, likely due to low membrane resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and an inference about the role of membrane resistance.

claim: The effect of increased firing in mitral cells appeared to plateau at light pulse durations ≥40 ms.
source: This effect appeared to plateau at light pulse durations ≥40 ms, even with 5 s continuous light pulse stimulation (data not shown), though at this duration, 1 of 5 cells tested exhibited depolarization block, while the remaining cells did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from extended light pulse stimulation experiments.

claim: At 40 ms pulse duration, 1 of 5 mitral cells tested exhibited depolarization block, while the remaining cells did not.
source: This effect appeared to plateau at light pulse durations ≥40 ms, even with 5 s continuous light pulse stimulation (data not shown), though at this duration, 1 of 5 cells tested exhibited depolarization block, while the remaining cells did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of mitral cells.

claim: Pyramidal cells were consistently driven at pulse widths up to 40 ms.
source: Pyramidal cells were consistently driven at pulse widths up to 40 ms (Figure 5E,F), but were more susceptible to depolarization block than mitral cells at longer pulse durations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of pyramidal cells.

claim: Pyramidal cells were more susceptible to depolarization block than mitral cells at longer pulse durations.
source: Pyramidal cells were consistently driven at pulse widths up to 40 ms (Figure 5E,F), but were more susceptible to depolarization block than mitral cells at longer pulse durations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data from recordings of pyramidal cells and mitral cells.

claim: Reduced light intensities attenuated average firing rates in mitral cells.
source: Though reduced light intensities attenuated average firing rates in mitral cells, consistent upward trends in firing were observed at all four light intensities, even at extended pulse durations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings at different light intensities.

claim: Consistent upward trends in firing were observed in mitral cells at all four light intensities, even at extended pulse durations.
source: Though reduced light intensities attenuated average firing rates in mitral cells, consistent upward trends in firing were observed at all four light intensities, even at extended pulse durations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings at different light intensities.

claim: Cortical pyramidal cells were more resistant to depolarization block than other interneurons tested, but also tended to display characteristic silencing beyond 40 ms.
source: Cortical pyramidal cells were more resistant to depolarization block than other interneurons tested, but also tended to display characteristic silencing beyond 40 ms (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative experimental data from recordings of pyramidal cells and interneurons.

claim: Mitral cells displayed modest amplitude reductions over the duration of a stimulus train during prolonged light pulses.
source: Similar to fast-spiking SST interneurons, mitral cells displayed modest amplitude reductions over the duration of a stimulus train during prolonged light pulses (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike amplitudes in mitral cells.

claim: Pyramidal cells exhibited slight amplitude reductions up to 40 ms pulse widths before drastic reductions were observed at longer durations.
source: Pyramidal cells exhibited slight amplitude reductions up to 40 ms pulse widths before drastic reductions were observed at longer durations (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike amplitudes in pyramidal cells.

claim: Brief light pulses were better at promoting higher spike fidelity in pyramidal cells.
source: Interestingly, while brief light pulses were better at promoting higher spike fidelity in pyramidal cells, they were often not sufficient for eliciting robust firing in mitral cells, resulting in reduced spike probability (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike fidelity in pyramidal cells.

claim: Brief light pulses were often not sufficient for eliciting robust firing in mitral cells, resulting in reduced spike probability.
source: Interestingly, while brief light pulses were better at promoting higher spike fidelity in pyramidal cells, they were often not sufficient for eliciting robust firing in mitral cells, resulting in reduced spike probability (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing spike probability in mitral cells.

claim: Extra spikes, particularly with longer pulses, were observed in all cell types.
source: Notably, extra spikes, particularly with longer pulses, were observed in all cell types.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data across all cell types tested.

claim: Minimal pulse widths for all cell types tested were determined to have sub-millisecond response kinetics.
source: In fact, minimal pulse widths for all cell types tested were determined to have sub-millisecond response kinetics (Figure 6F), likely contributing to the observation of spike doublets and triplets when neurons were stimulated with long pulses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring minimal pulse widths required for spiking.

claim: Different neuronal subtypes respond with drastically different response kinetics when stimulated with ChR2.
source: Together, these data show that different neuronal subtypes respond with drastically different response kinetics when stimulated with ChR2, and that the proper photostimulation parameters should be determined to elicit the desired firing output in target neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative experimental data from multiple neuronal subtypes.

claim: The potential for unknowingly silencing neurons that express ChR2 is greatest when firing properties of targeted neurons are not recorded simultaneously with light exposure.
source: The potential for unknowingly silencing neurons that express ChR2 is greatest when firing properties of targeted neurons are not recorded simultaneously with light exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and their implications for experimental design.

claim: Regular-spiking SST interneurons exhibited robust silencing due to prolonged light pulse duration in vivo.
source: Consistent with observations made in slices, regular-spiking SST interneurons exhibited robust silencing due to prolonged light pulse duration (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data.

claim: Presumptive pyramidal cell firing was effectively inhibited by ChR2-expressing SST interneurons activated by short light pulse durations.
source: Though in vivo paired recordings were not made, presumptive pyramidal cell firing was effectively inhibited by ChR2-expressing SST interneurons activated by short light pulse durations, while pyramidal cell firing returned to baseline upon depolarization block of SST interneurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data showing changes in presumptive pyramidal cell activity.

claim: Pyramidal cell firing returned to baseline upon depolarization block of SST interneurons.
source: Though in vivo paired recordings were not made, presumptive pyramidal cell firing was effectively inhibited by ChR2-expressing SST interneurons activated by short light pulse durations, while pyramidal cell firing returned to baseline upon depolarization block of SST interneurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data showing changes in presumptive pyramidal cell activity.

claim: Increasing light pulse duration onto fast-spiking SST cortical interneurons led to enhanced firing.
source: The opposite effect was observed in fast-spiking SST cortical interneurons. Increasing light pulse duration onto these interneurons led to enhanced firing (Figure 7C) and enhanced inhibition of presumptive cortical pyramidal cells with increasing pulse duration (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data from fast-spiking SST interneurons.
